\chapter{Pleasure, Reason, Respect}
\label{ch:placer-y-consejo}
\hlchaptermodality{321}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer a first meeting with un placer, agree with tienes razon, and ask for patience, respect or advice in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C321-consejo: answer mucho gusto with un placer, hand somebody razon, and ask for paciencia and un consejo.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el placer]{el placer — the answer to a first meeting}

\label{lesson:ES-C321-placer}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{good luck}, then \emph{it is my fault}. (\emph{¡Buena suerte!}; \emph{es mi culpa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mucho gusto — this word answers it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pla-CER}, stress on the last beat. The \emph{pl} runs straight together. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el placer} — \textquotedblleft{}pleasure.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{placēre} meant \emph{to please}, and it is one of the most productive words Latin ever handed on. Watch how far it reaches in English.

\textbf{Please} and \textbf{pleasure} came the long way through French and kept the plain meaning. \textbf{Placid} came straight off the Latin and means \emph{pleasing}, which turned into \emph{calm}, because what does not disturb you pleases you. A \textbf{plea} in a court is what you set down hoping it will please. And a \textbf{placebo} is the Latin sentence \emph{I shall please} — a thing given because it will satisfy, not because it will cure.

\emph{Placer} is also the doing-word: \emph{me place} is an old, formal way to say \emph{it pleases me}. But the piece you want is the naming one.

When somebody says \emph{mucho gusto} on meeting you, the reply you will hear over and over is \emph{\textbf{un placer}} — \emph{a pleasure}. Three syllables that do the whole job.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second thing to say when you meet somebody, so the exchange is not one line repeated back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el placer}
  \item \emph{un placer}
  \item \emph{un placer — buena suerte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{placebo} mean, word for word? (\emph{I shall please}.) What do you answer when somebody says \emph{mucho gusto}? (\emph{Un placer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la razón]{la razón — being right is having something}

\label{lesson:ES-C321-razon}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{it is my fault}, then \emph{a pleasure}. (\emph{Es mi culpa}; \emph{un placer}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ra-ZÓN}, stress on the last beat — and the written accent is there to say so. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la razón} — \textquotedblleft{}reason.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ratio}, in its other form \textbf{rationem}, was a reckoning: a count, a calculation, the running of an account. Only afterwards did it come to mean the faculty that does the counting.

English holds both ends at once. A \textbf{ratio} is still a bare reckoning of one number against another. A \textbf{ration} is an amount reckoned out to you. \textbf{Rational} and \textbf{reason} are the thinking end — and \emph{reason} is that same Latin word after a long walk through French.

Spanish did the same thing to itself. \emph{Rationem} worn down slowly through speech became \emph{\textbf{razón}}. The very same word picked up later out of a book became \textbf{ración}, a portion. Two Spanish words, one Latin ancestor, one of them weathered and one of them fresh.

Then comes the useful part. Spanish does not say \emph{you are right}. It says \emph{\textbf{tienes razón}} — \emph{you have reason}. Being right is holding something, the way a fault is something you hold. And \emph{no tienes razón} hands it back.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to agree with somebody that is stronger than \emph{sí}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la razón}
  \item \emph{tienes razón}
  \item \emph{tienes razón — es mi culpa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{ratio} mean before it meant thinking? (A reckoning, a count.) How does Spanish say \emph{you are right}? (\emph{Tienes razón} — you have reason.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el respeto]{el respeto — turning to look again}

\label{lesson:ES-C321-respeto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a pleasure}, then \emph{you are right}. (\emph{Un placer}; \emph{tienes razón}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{res-PE-to}, stress on the middle beat. The \emph{s} and \emph{p} meet with no vowel between. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el respeto} — \textquotedblleft{}respect.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart and it is a movement of the eyes. Latin \textbf{specere} was \emph{to look}. Put \textbf{re-} in front, \emph{back} or \emph{again}, and \textbf{respicere} is \emph{to look back at}. A \textbf{respectus} was that second look: you had walked past, and you turned.

That is what the word still carries. To respect somebody is to give them the look you do not give to furniture.

\emph{Specere} is everywhere in English once you can see it. A \textbf{spectacle} is a thing to be looked at. \textbf{Spectacles} are what you look through. To \textbf{inspect} is to look into, to \textbf{suspect} is to look from underneath, and a \textbf{spectator} does nothing but look. English also has \textbf{respite} — a pause — which is the same \emph{respectus} down a different road: a moment when you get to look back.

Spanish keeps a near-twin, \emph{respecto}, for \emph{with regard to}. The one you want here is \emph{respeto}, with no second \emph{c}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word whose shape tells you what to do with your attention.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el respeto}
  \item \emph{con respeto}
  \item \emph{con respeto — tienes razón}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{respicere} mean, piece by piece? (To look back at.) Name two English words built on \emph{specere}. (\emph{Spectacle}, \emph{inspect}, \emph{spectator}, \emph{suspect}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la paciencia]{la paciencia — the word for going through it}

\label{lesson:ES-C321-paciencia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{you are right}, then \emph{with respect}. (\emph{Tienes razón}; \emph{con respeto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item -ncia — the ending on the end of this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-CIEN-cia}, stress on the middle. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is a plain \emph{s} across the Americas. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la paciencia} — \textquotedblleft{}patience.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{patī} meant \emph{to undergo}, \emph{to have something happen to you}. Not to wait pleasantly — to be on the receiving end. \textbf{Patientia} was the capacity to take it.

Which explains a word you have used all your life without hearing it. In a hospital, a \textbf{patient} is not somebody being calm. A patient is the one the treatment is happening \emph{to}. Everyone else in the room is doing; one person is undergoing, and that person is named for it.

The same \emph{patī} went into Church Latin and came out as \textbf{passion} — which originally meant \emph{suffering}, not enthusiasm. \textbf{Compassion} is \emph{undergoing with}: standing in it beside somebody. And something \textbf{passive} is a thing things are done to.

The ending is the \emph{-ncia} you already know, the one that turns a way of being into a thing you can name and hand over. \emph{Paciencia, por favor} asks somebody for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you can ask for out loud when you need another minute.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la paciencia}
  \item \emph{paciencia, por favor}
  \item \emph{con respeto — paciencia}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{patī} mean? (To undergo.) Why is a hospital patient called that? (They are the one the treatment happens to.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el consejo]{el consejo — ten words, and a road you have walked before}

\label{lesson:ES-C321-consejo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{with respect}, then \emph{patience, please}. (\emph{Con respeto}; \emph{paciencia, por favor}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el ajo — the same sound change made this word too.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{con-SE-jo}. The \emph{j} is the jota, a breath scraped at the back of the mouth. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el consejo} — \textquotedblleft{}advice.\textquotedblright{} And also \textquotedblleft{}a council.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{consilium} was a sitting-together to decide: both the deliberation and the body of people doing it. Spanish kept the pair. \emph{Un consejo} is a piece of advice; \emph{el consejo} can be the board that meets. Advice, in Spanish, still sounds faintly like a committee.

English split them and then mixed them up. \textbf{Counsel} is the advising — \emph{counsel for the defence}. A \textbf{council} is the body. Two spellings, one Latin word, and speakers have been confusing them ever since.

Now the ending, because you have walked this road once. \emph{Allium} became \emph{ajo}: the \emph{-lium} collapsed into a jota. \textbf{Consilium} did the same thing — \emph{consilium}, \emph{consejo}. Once a Latin \emph{l} stood before an \emph{i} and another vowel, Spanish pulled it back into the throat.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ten courtesy words. The first five name what politeness handles: the good turn, the weight, the cost, the token drawn and the fault. These five name what you offer back: the pleasure, the reckoning, the second look, the undergoing, and the sitting-down-together.

Not one of them is a set phrase. Each is a thing you can put where you need it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el consejo}
  \item \emph{un consejo, por favor}
  \item \emph{paciencia y respeto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things does \emph{consejo} name? (Advice, and a council.) Which earlier word took the same \emph{-lium} road to a jota? (\emph{Ajo}, from \emph{allium}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
